approach_notes: Sampled 2,304 prompts; filtered out 78 auto-injected SSOT/preflight blocks to focus on user-authored content (2,226 prompts). Ran node scripts to count exact-substring document-frequency for every trigger phrase listed below, and read 25+ representative samples in full to validate that each cluster is structural (authoring shape) rather than topical.

recognition_modes.name: ASCII architecture diagram as the spec
recognition_modes.description: User has already drawn the system in box-art and arrows; the diagram itself is the design — code should mirror it node-for-node.
structural_markers: Unicode box-drawing characters (┌ ┐ └ ┘ ─ │ ├ ┤)
Tree-style file hierarchies using ├── and └──
Vertical arrow flow ▼ between named subsystems
Code-fence enclosing the diagram (```...```)
Heading like '## Architecture' or '## Module Structure' immediately above
recognition_modes.what_it_means: The user has already done the design work. They want the code laid out exactly like the diagram — same module names, same edges, same direction of flow. They are not asking for opinions on the architecture.
automatic_actions: Treat each labeled box as a required module/struct/file with the exact name shown
Treat arrows as the only allowed dependency edges; do not introduce shortcuts or back-edges
Mirror file-tree diagrams 1:1 — create exactly those files in exactly those directories
Quote the diagram back at the top of the implementation as a comment or doc-block so drift is visible
If something in the diagram is impossible, surface that single fact and stop, do not silently substitute
anti_patterns: Proposing an alternate layering 'for cleanliness'
Renaming boxes (e.g. 'I called it FooHandler instead of FooSlot')
Adding intermediate adapters or facades the diagram does not show
Asking which box should be implemented first when the arrows imply a topological order
Skipping a box because 'we can stub it later'
example_paraphrases: ## Module Structure with a fenced file-tree showing engine/src/lexicon/ subdirs and impl files; the tree is the layout to create.
User flow box → trait box → impl box → output box, with vertical arrows; the diagram is the entire prompt.
recognition_modes.promote_to: skill — 'mirror-the-diagram' enforces 1:1 layout; the trigger (box-drawing chars in fenced code) is unambiguous.

recognition_modes.name: Source-of-truth comparison table
recognition_modes.description: User authors a markdown table that is itself the canonical mapping (subsystem → backend → device → strategy, or feature → file → status); rows are commitments, not suggestions.
structural_markers: Pipe-delimited markdown table with `|---|---|` header separator
First column is a stable identifier (Profile, Subsystem, Concern, Field, Crate)
Second/third columns assign ownership, file path, or status
Often introduced by a heading like '## Slot Table', '## What Is NOT In X', or 'SSOT'
recognition_modes.what_it_means: The user has settled the contract. Each row is a decision already made. They want code that exactly populates that table — same identifiers, same assignments, no extra rows, no merged/dropped rows.
automatic_actions: Treat each row as a test case: every identifier in column 1 must resolve in code with the values in subsequent columns
When generating code, use the column-1 identifiers verbatim as struct/enum/const names
If a row says 'lives in X', put it in X — don't reorganize
When verifying, walk the table top-to-bottom and report row-by-row pass/fail
Echo the table back at the end of the change with a status column appended
anti_patterns: Adding rows the user didn't author ('I also added a default row for…')
Collapsing rows that look similar
Renaming the column-1 identifier to something 'more idiomatic'
Re-deriving the mapping from first principles instead of obeying the table
Asking 'are you sure about row N?' when the table is already specific
example_paraphrases: Three-column table mapping each profile to a fixed backend and a fixed voice line.
Table mapping every cross-cutting concern to a single owning module path.
recognition_modes.promote_to: skill — 'obey-the-table' applies on any prompt with a markdown table whose header has a separator row.

recognition_modes.name: Rust struct/enum/trait pasted as the spec
recognition_modes.description: User pastes the exact public types they want — field names, variant names, and signatures are the contract. The implementation just has to satisfy that shape.
structural_markers: Code fence with `rust` language tag
Contains `pub struct`, `pub enum`, `pub trait`, or `pub fn` definitions
Field/variant doc-comments using `///` describing intended semantics
Often paired with an enclosing heading naming the subsystem
recognition_modes.what_it_means: The user has chosen the public surface. They want that surface kept verbatim — same names, same casing, same generics — and the body filled in to honor the doc-comments.
automatic_actions: Use the exact identifiers from the paste — including casing and ordering of fields/variants
Preserve every `///` doc-comment as written into the final file
If a field's type is ambiguous, pick the minimal-dependency stdlib choice and call out the choice in the report
Place the type in the module the surrounding heading implies (no relocation)
Add only what the doc-comments demand; do not invent extra public methods
anti_patterns: Renaming a variant for 'consistency'
Reordering fields to match an alphabetic or 'natural' order
Switching `String` to `&str`, `Vec<T>` to `SmallVec<T>`, etc., without being asked
Wrapping the struct in `Arc<RwLock<…>>` 'for thread safety' when the spec didn't
Adding `#[derive(...)]` lines the user didn't include unless required to compile
example_paraphrases: User pastes a `pub struct` with documented fields; implementation has to honor those names exactly.
User pastes a `pub struct BackendPool` with a documented `get_or_load` method showing the ref-count semantics — body must match the doc-comments.
recognition_modes.promote_to: skill — fires on any code-fence containing `pub struct|enum|trait|fn`; tells Claude to honor the surface verbatim.

recognition_modes.name: Pre-authored phased execution plan
recognition_modes.description: User has already broken the work into Phase 0..N with files-touched, diff-shape, and verify commands per phase; the prompt is asking for execution, not redesign.
structural_markers: Headings of the form `## Phase N — <name>` or `### Phase A`
Per-phase 'Files:' line with bulleted file paths
Per-phase fenced bash block with `cargo check`, `cargo test`, `pnpm check`, or `git diff`
Numbered execution-order section at the end
Sometimes a final '## Verification gate' tying phases together
recognition_modes.what_it_means: The user has already done the planning skill's job. They want literal execution of phase 0, then a stop, then phase 1, etc. — not a re-plan, not a merged super-phase, not a parallelized variant.
automatic_actions: Execute exactly one phase per turn unless the user says otherwise
Touch only the files listed under that phase's 'Files:' bullet
Run the verify block as written, paste the output, and stop at the gate
Report results per-phase using the user's phase numbering and headings
If a verify command fails, fix the cause inside that phase's file list — do not pull from later phases
anti_patterns: Combining phases ('I did 0, 1, and 2 in one commit')
Substituting a different verify command
Adding a 'Phase 0.5' the user didn't author
Re-running the planning skill on top of a prompt that is already a plan
Touching files outside the phase's listed set 'while I'm in there'
example_paraphrases: Phase 0 — commit the merge (one file, run cargo check); Phase 1 — wire the new flag (three files, cargo test then pnpm check); Phase 2 — UI surface (two svelte files, svelte-check).
Phase A depends on STOP 1-3; Phase B depends on Phase A; Phase C is the verification aggregator added last.
recognition_modes.promote_to: skill — 'execute-the-phases' fires on any prompt with two or more `Phase N` headings each owning a file list.

recognition_modes.name: Sprint-close verification checklist
recognition_modes.description: User has authored the exact `[ ]` checklist that defines done; sprint is closed only when each box is provably checked.
structural_markers: Heading `## Verification Checklist`, `## Verification Gate`, or `Verification gates`
Markdown checkboxes `- [ ]` or `- [x]`
Items reference concrete commands (cargo, pnpm, lefthook) or concrete behavior (set X → reload → see Y)
Sometimes paired with a 'Zero errors means zero' statement
recognition_modes.what_it_means: The user has fully specified the success criteria. They are not asking what 'done' means — they are asking Claude to walk that list and prove each item.
automatic_actions: Run each item in order; capture the literal command output
Report back as the same list with [x] or [ ] flipped, not a prose summary
Treat warnings as failures unless the item explicitly carves out 'errors only'
If an item fails, fix it before marking the next item
Do not invent additional checklist items
anti_patterns: Marking [x] without running the underlying command
Skipping items the user wrote because 'they look redundant'
Summarizing 'mostly green' instead of listing each box
Adding 'I also checked Z' items the user didn't author
Treating a pre-existing baseline error as 'not in scope'
example_paraphrases: ## Verification Checklist (sprint close) — boxes for STOPs answered, dead code gone, project_path round-trips, cargo check passes, pnpm check passes, lefthook pre-commit passes, ip-boundary lint passes.
## Verification gates — fenced bash with cargo check / cargo test / svelte-check / biome / xtask run-dev, plus 'zero errors means zero'.
recognition_modes.promote_to: skill — 'walk-the-checklist' fires whenever a prompt contains three or more `- [ ]` items under a verification heading.

recognition_modes.name: Frozen-surface declaration
recognition_modes.description: User explicitly enumerates files/modules that are correct and must not be edited; the change is constrained to everything else.
structural_markers: Heading like `## DO NOT TOUCH THESE FILES (they're correct):` or `### Do not touch`
Bulleted list of file paths underneath
Often immediately follows a 'situation report' that explains why those files are good
Sometimes accompanied by 'Out of scope' / 'Deferred' sibling sections
recognition_modes.what_it_means: The user has localized the bug to a known surface and is protecting the parts that are working. They want surgical edits with a hard fence around the protected list.
automatic_actions: Treat each path in the protected list as read-only — read it, but do not write to it
Before any write, confirm the target path is NOT under the protected list
When listing files in the response, group changes as 'Touched (allowed)' vs 'Read-only (protected, cited only)'
If the fix appears to require touching a protected file, stop and surface that conflict instead of doing it
Mirror the user's framing in the report: confirm which protected files were re-read but not modified
anti_patterns: Editing a protected file 'just to fix a small import'
Refactoring a protected file 'while I'm there'
Asking 'should I touch X?' when X is on the list — the answer is already no
Rewriting a protected file in a different style and claiming it's equivalent
Expanding scope into 'deferred' items in the same change
example_paraphrases: Frontend wizard is well-built — DO NOT TOUCH SetupWizard.svelte, ModelsStep.svelte, the bindings; problem is entirely in the Rust commands behind the bindings.
Out of scope: model swap UX, telemetry spans, OAuth flow, code indexer — those are separate sprints.
recognition_modes.promote_to: skill — 'frozen-surface' fires on 'do not touch' / 'out of scope' / 'deferred' headings; enforces a write-allowlist for the turn.

recognition_modes.name: Pasted compiler/check output as the task
recognition_modes.description: User pastes the verbatim error output from cargo / svelte-check / biome / tsc; the implicit ask is 'fix this exact diagnostic, nothing else'.
structural_markers: Verbatim `error[E####]` Rust diagnostic with file:line:col
`svelte-check` report with `Cannot find module '$lib/...'` style messages
JSON diagnostic blob with `resource`, `severity`, `message`, `startLineNumber`
PowerShell prompt suffix `PS {repo}/...>` indicating raw terminal paste
Rarely any prose around it; the paste IS the prompt
recognition_modes.what_it_means: The user has the output in front of them. They want triage on this exact diagnostic with the exact code reference cited — not a refactor proposal, not a 'while I was looking' tour.
automatic_actions: Open the file:line cited in the diagnostic first; read enough to identify the root cause
State the cause in one or two sentences before proposing the fix
Limit the fix to the file(s) the diagnostic cites unless a structural cause forces a sibling edit (and call that out)
Re-run the same command the user pasted from and paste the new output back
If multiple diagnostics are pasted, fix them in the order they appear and report each as resolved
anti_patterns: Dragging in unrelated cleanups
Suggesting a tooling/version change instead of fixing the code
'Refactoring the module while I'm here'
Glossing over the diagnostic with a higher-level redesign
Skipping the re-run — leaving the user to verify
example_paraphrases: User pastes a single `error[E0432]: unresolved import` from cargo with no surrounding text.
User pastes a JSON svelte-check resource saying `Cannot find module '$lib/sys/generated/bindings.js'` — fix is to regen bindings or correct the import path.
recognition_modes.promote_to: skill — 'fix-this-diagnostic' fires on `error[E####]` or svelte-check JSON; constrains scope to cited files.

recognition_modes.name: Fork with stated hypothesis
recognition_modes.description: User describes a decision they're about to make and explicitly invites correction with their reasoning attached — 'my thought was X, am I wrong?'
structural_markers: Phrases of the form 'my thought was…', 'I thought… right?', 'am I wrong?'
Often a comparison frame: 'X or should it be Y'
Mentions a domain rule or best-practice belief the user already holds
Usually short (under 500 chars) — pure decision-mode, not an implementation request
recognition_modes.what_it_means: The user has a working hypothesis and wants confirmation OR a stern correction with reasoning. They are not asking for options; they are asking for a yes/no on their position with a one-paragraph rationale.
automatic_actions: Answer the yes/no first, in one sentence — confirm or correct the hypothesis
Cite the actual rule/code/standard that decides it (file:line if internal, doc URL if external)
If wrong, correct sternly with the right answer; do not soften or hedge
If right, say 'yes — and here's why' in one or two sentences, then proceed to execute on it
Do not produce a multi-option menu when one position is already named
anti_patterns: Listing three or four 'approaches' with pros/cons
Bouncing the question back ('it depends on your goals…')
Confirming the hypothesis without checking — sycophancy
Refusing to commit because 'both are valid' when they are not equivalent in this codebase
Burying the answer at the end of a long preamble
example_paraphrases: I wanted Rust to own the route since I thought best practice said it should — am I wrong?
Runtime and build are essentially the same for Svelte 5, just a dev gate, so we shouldn't hack it in — that's right, isn't it?
recognition_modes.promote_to: none — handle inline; promoting risks over-formalizing what is already a one-question decision.
